notes.meaning: Jesus tells a story about a man who planted a vineyard with a fence, wine vat, and watchtower, and leased it to farmers before traveling away. The story echoes an old song from the prophet Isaiah where the vineyard is Israel. God had prepared everything His people needed to flourish and placed leaders in charge to care for them.

When harvest season arrived, the owner sent a servant to collect his rightful share of the grapes. In those days, a vineyard owner waited several years for the first crop before asking for his rent. In the same way, God patiently expected a harvest of righteousness and faith from His people.

Instead of paying their rent, the tenant farmers seized the servant, beat him, and sent him away with nothing. They wanted to enjoy the benefits of the vineyard without answering to the owner. This pictures how Israel's leaders mistreated God's early prophets and refused to offer the spiritual fruit God asked for.

The owner sent another servant, but the farmers struck him on the head and treated him with cruel insults. Their defiance grew worse each time an agent came to speak for the owner. Throughout the Old Testament, faithful messengers of God faced stoning, beatings, and shameful rejection by their own people.

The owner sent yet another servant, and this one they murdered. He kept sending many others over time, but the tenants beat some and killed others. This shows the incredible patience of God, who sent prophet after prophet even while Israel's rulers hardened their hearts in rebellion.

The owner had only one person left to send: his own dearly loved son. He decided to send him last, believing the tenants would finally show respect to his heir. Jesus was speaking of Himself, showing that He is not just another messenger, but God's unique Son sent to earth.

When the tenants saw the son coming, they plotted together to kill him so the vineyard would become theirs. They may have thought the owner was dead and that removing the only heir would leave the land open for the taking. This reveals the greed and rebellion in the human heart, wanting God's gifts while trying to push God aside.

The farmers grabbed the son, killed him, and tossed his body outside the vineyard. Leaving someone unburied was an act of complete contempt and dishonor. Jesus was plainly describing how the religious leaders would soon take Him and put Him to death outside the city gates.

Jesus asks what the owner will do, and answers that he will come destroy the wicked tenants and hand the vineyard to others. The corrupt leaders who rejected God's messengers would face divine judgment. God would entrust the spiritual care of His kingdom to new leaders, opening the door wide to the nations.

Jesus points His listeners to Psalm 118, where a rejected stone ends up becoming the most important stone in the building. The religious builders regarded Jesus as useless and threw Him aside. Yet God chose Him to be the cornerstone, the main stone holding the whole house of God together.

Quoting further from the psalm, Jesus declares that this reversal was done by the Lord and is amazing to see. The rulers thought their rejection of Jesus would be the end of Him, but God turned it into His greatest victory. God's people can only look with wonder at how He brings triumph out of suffering.

The Jewish leaders wanted to arrest Jesus immediately because they understood that the parable of the wicked farmers was aimed directly at them. Even so, fear of the enthusiastic crowd kept them from laying hands on Him. They walked away frustrated, looking for a quieter way to destroy Him.

The rulers sent some Pharisees and Herodians to trap Jesus in His own words. These two groups usually disliked each other, because the Pharisees hated Roman rule while the Herodians supported Rome's puppet kings. Their shared opposition to Jesus brought them together into an uneasy alliance.

The spies tried to flatter Jesus, calling Him an honest teacher who speaks God's truth without worrying about anyone's opinion. Then they asked their trap question: is it right under God's law to pay taxes to the Roman emperor Caesar? If Jesus said yes, the Jewish crowd would view Him as a traitor, but if He said no, Rome could execute Him for rebellion.

Jesus saw right through their fake compliments and called out their dishonest motives. He asked why they were trying to trap Him and told them to bring Him a silver coin called a denarius. Instead of dodging the question, He prepared to teach a deeper truth about duty and worship.

When they brought the coin, Jesus asked whose portrait and name were stamped on it. They answered that it belonged to Caesar, the Roman emperor. By using Caesar's money in daily life, they had already accepted the benefits and authority of his government.

Jesus told them to give back to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to give to God what is God's. Christians owe legitimate civil duties and taxes to earthly rulers, but our whole heart and worship belong only to the Lord. His enemies were left completely stunned by His wisdom and could find no fault in Him.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Human beings bear God's image, so Caesar himself is subject to God. This means citizens are required in conscience to disobey civil authorities whenever government demands violate God's moral law.

notes.meaning: Next, members of the Sadducees came to question Jesus. The Sadducees were a wealthy group who held power in the temple and denied that people will ever rise from the dead. They approached Jesus with an imaginary scenario designed to make the resurrection look ridiculous.

They cited a rule from the books of Moses that protected a family's name and land. If a married man died without children, his brother was supposed to marry the widow and have a child in his brother's memory. The Sadducees used this ancient command to set up their clever riddle.

They told a story about seven brothers where the oldest brother married a wife and died without leaving any children. According to the law, this left the widow childless and placed the duty of marriage onto the next brother. The Sadducees started with this common first step to build up their extreme puzzle.

The second brother married the widow to raise up a family for his dead brother, but he also died leaving no children. The third brother married her next, and the exact same thing happened to him. The questioners kept repeating the tragedy down the line to make the problem seem impossible to untangle.

All seven brothers ended up marrying the woman in turn, and none of them left any children behind. Finally, after outliving every husband, the woman herself died. The Sadducees believed this absurd situation proved that bodily resurrection after death could not possibly make sense.
